entries.text: Resting heart rate (RHR) for adults is typically 60–100 bpm; well-trained people often sit at 40–60 bpm. A sustained RHR above 100 bpm at rest, or below 40 bpm with dizziness, fatigue or fainting, is worth a doctor's review. Within the normal range, a lower RHR goes with better fitness: in large cohorts every 10 bpm higher RHR is linked to about 9% higher all-cause mortality.

entries.topic: Resting heart rate against your baseline
entries.text: Compare resting heart rate with your own 30-day baseline, not with other people. A rise of 3–5 bpm for a day or two commonly follows short sleep, alcohol, dehydration, heat, stress or hard training. A rise of 5–10 bpm for several days, especially with higher wrist temperature or breathing rate, often comes before an infection. A slow fall over weeks usually reflects improving aerobic fitness.
entries.source: Radin et al., Lancet Digit Health 2020; Mishra et al., Nat Biomed Eng 2020

entries.text: Apple Watch reports heart rate variability as SDNN in milliseconds, measured in short readings and overnight. Values differ a lot between people (roughly 20–100+ ms in adults) and fall with age, so a single number says little; the trend against your own baseline matters. HRV above your baseline signals good parasympathetic recovery.

Read HRV as a percentage of your 30-day baseline: within about ±10% is normal day-to-day noise; 10–25% below suggests incomplete recovery; more than 25% below for two or more days points to strain, illness or poor sleep and calls for an easier day. A 7-day rolling average is more reliable than one night.

Things that reliably lower next-morning HRV: alcohol (even 1–2 drinks), late heavy meals, short or irregular sleep, dehydration, a high training load, psychological stress, illness and heat. Things that raise it over weeks: regular aerobic exercise, consistent sleep timing, slow-breathing practice, and lower body fat.

Maximum heart rate is commonly estimated as 220 − age or, more accurately for adults, 208 − 0.7 × age (Tanaka). Individuals differ from either formula by about ±10–12 bpm, so an observed peak in a hard effort is better when known.

Zones by heart-rate reserve (Karvonen: target = resting + % × (max − resting)): zone 1 50–60% recovery, zone 2 60–70% easy aerobic base, zone 3 70–80% tempo, zone 4 80–90% threshold, zone 5 90–100% maximal. For health and endurance most weekly time belongs in zones 1–2.

Heart-rate recovery — the drop in the first minute after stopping hard exercise — is a fitness marker. A fall of 12 bpm or less in one minute with an upright cool-down is linked to higher cardiovascular risk; fit people often drop 20–30 bpm or more.

Occasional skipped or extra beats (ectopics) are common and usually harmless, often triggered by caffeine, alcohol, stress, poor sleep or dehydration. Get a medical review if palpitations last more than a few minutes, are fast and irregular, or come with chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness or fainting.

An Apple Watch irregular-rhythm notification means repeated readings suggested atrial fibrillation (AF). AF raises stroke risk about five-fold, so a notification should lead to a medical review and an ECG; record a 30-second ECG on the watch to bring along. The watch cannot detect heart attacks.

AHA/ACC 2017: normal below 120/80 mmHg; elevated 120–129 and below 80; stage 1 hypertension 130–139 or 80–89; stage 2 140+ or 90+; hypertensive crisis above 180 and/or above 120. Chinese (2024) and European guidelines define hypertension as 140/90 or more measured in clinic, and home readings of 135/85 or more also count as high. A diagnosis needs repeated readings on separate days, not one value.

For an accurate home reading: no caffeine, exercise or smoking for 30 minutes, empty bladder, sit for 5 minutes with back supported and feet flat, arm resting at heart level, cuff on the bare upper arm, no talking. Take two readings one minute apart and average them; measure morning and evening for 7 days before judging.
entries.source: AHA Scientific Statement on Home BP 2019

entries.text: Measured effects on systolic pressure: weight loss about −1 mmHg per kg lost; DASH-style diet −11 mmHg in people with hypertension; cutting sodium by about 1 g a day −5 to −6; more potassium from vegetables and fruit −4 to −5; 90–150 min of aerobic exercise a week −5 to −8; isometric or resistance training −4 to −5; limiting alcohol −4.

Blood pressure below about 90/60 mmHg is only a problem when it causes symptoms such as dizziness, blurred vision or fainting. Drinking enough, standing up slowly and avoiding long hot showers help; new low pressure with symptoms, especially on a new medicine, should be reviewed.

Orthostatic hypotension is a drop of 20+ mmHg systolic or 10+ mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing. Light-headedness on standing is common after dehydration, alcohol, heat or long bed rest; frequent episodes, falls or fainting need a doctor's check, especially in older adults or people on blood-pressure medicines.

Normal blood oxygen saturation at sea level is 95–100%. Readings of 91–94% deserve a repeat at rest with warm hands and a still wrist; a reliable reading of 90% or below, especially with breathlessness, needs prompt medical attention.

Brief dips into the low 90s during sleep are common. Repeated drops below 90%, together with loud snoring, gasping, morning headaches or daytime sleepiness, suggest sleep apnea and are worth raising with a doctor.

Blood oxygen falls with altitude: around 2,500 m readings of 90–95% are normal, and above 3,500 m healthy people can read in the mid-80s. Headache, nausea and poor sleep after going above 2,500 m suggest acute mountain sickness: stop ascending. Breathlessness at rest, confusion or unsteady walking means descend at once.

Wrist oximetry is less accurate than a fingertip clip: cold skin, tattoos, a loose band, movement and darker skin pigmentation can distort readings. Trust repeated readings at rest and trends rather than a single value.

A normal adult respiratory rate at rest is 12–20 breaths per minute; during sleep the watch typically reads 12–18. A sustained rise of 2–3 breaths/min above your baseline can be an early sign of infection or, with a high resting heart rate, of overreaching.
entries.source: Clinical reference ranges; Natarajan et al. 2020

entries.text: Apple Watch wrist temperature is a deviation from your own baseline measured during sleep, not body temperature. Shifts within ±0.5 °C are normal; +0.5 to +1 °C over two nights can come from alcohol, a warm room, illness or the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle; above +1 °C together with a raised resting heart rate often signals fever.
entries.source: Apple; Mason et al., Sci Rep 2022

entries.text: Normal body temperature is about 36.1–37.2 °C. In China 37.3 °C or more (armpit) is called fever: 37.3–38.0 °C low-grade, 38.1–39.0 °C moderate, 39.1–41.0 °C high, and above 41 °C hyperpyrexia, an emergency. Below 35 °C is hypothermia.

For a fever: rest, drink fluids, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen as directed on the label if uncomfortable. See a doctor if fever lasts more than 3 days, goes above 39.5 °C, or comes with a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade under pressure, confusion, chest pain, breathlessness or severe headache.

After ovulation, wrist and basal temperature rise by about 0.2–0.5 °C and stay up through the luteal phase until the period; resting heart rate may be 2–4 bpm higher and HRV a little lower in that phase. This is normal and not a sign of illness.
entries.source: Shilaih et al. 2018; Apple Women's Health Study

entries.text: Recommended sleep: adults 18–64 need 7–9 hours, adults 65+ 7–8 hours, teenagers 13–18 8–10 hours. Regularly sleeping under 7 hours is linked to weight gain, high blood pressure, diabetes, depression and weaker immunity; regularly needing more than 9 hours can signal poor sleep quality or illness.

An adult night cycles about every 90 minutes through light sleep (N1/N2, about 50–60% of the night), deep sleep (N3, about 13–23%, mostly in the first half) and REM (about 20–25%, mostly in the second half). For 7.5 hours that is roughly 60–100 minutes of deep and 90–120 minutes of REM. Wearables estimate stages from movement and heart rate, so treat stage minutes as approximate.

Deep sleep supports physical recovery, growth-hormone release and memory, and it declines with age. Alcohol, late caffeine, a warm bedroom, late intense exercise and irregular bedtimes reduce it; consistent sleep timing, daytime activity and a cool (about 16–19 °C), dark room help.

REM sleep supports emotional processing and learning and is concentrated in the last third of the night, so cutting the morning short loses REM first. Alcohol strongly suppresses REM in the first half of the night.
entries.source: Ebrahim et al., Alcohol Clin Exp Res 2013

entries.text: Sleep regularity — going to bed and waking at similar times (within 30–60 minutes), weekends included — predicts health and mortality as strongly as sleep duration in large studies. Shifting by 2 or more hours at weekends ("social jet lag") worsens the following week's sleep and metabolic markers.

Caffeine has a half-life of about 5 hours (range 2–10), so a 200 mg coffee at 16:00 still leaves about 100 mg at 21:00. Stop caffeine at least 8 hours before bed if sleep is light or short. Up to 400 mg a day (about 4 cups of brewed coffee) is considered safe for healthy adults; in pregnancy the limit is 200 mg a day.
entries.source: EFSA 2015; FDA; Gardiner et al., Sleep Med Rev 2023

entries.text: Alcohol helps people fall asleep but fragments the second half of the night, suppresses REM, raises resting heart rate by several bpm and lowers HRV; wearables show it after even 1–2 drinks. Finish drinking at least 3–4 hours before bed.
entries.source: Pietilä et al., JMIR Ment Health 2018

entries.text: Naps of 10–20 minutes before about 15:00 improve alertness without hurting night sleep. Naps over 30 minutes bring grogginess, and long late naps delay bedtime; frequent long daytime naps in older adults can signal poor night sleep.

Morning outdoor light (10–30 minutes, even when cloudy) anchors the body clock and makes falling asleep easier at night. In the last 1–2 hours before bed, dim screens and overhead lights; reducing brightness and engagement matters more than blue-light filters.
entries.source: Blume et al. 2019; Chang et al., PNAS 2015

entries.text: Core habits: a fixed wake time, bed only for sleep, a cool dark quiet room, no heavy meals 2–3 hours before bed, no intense exercise in the last 1–2 hours, a 30–60 minute wind-down, and getting up if still awake after about 20 minutes.

Insomnia is trouble falling or staying asleep at least 3 nights a week for 3 months with daytime effects. CBT-I (sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive techniques) is the first-line treatment and lasts longer than sleeping pills; digital CBT-I programs work too.

Signs of obstructive sleep apnea: loud snoring, witnessed pauses or gasping, waking with a dry mouth or headache, daytime sleepiness, and blood pressure that is hard to control. Risk rises with neck size, weight, age and alcohol. It is diagnosed with a sleep study and is very treatable; untreated it raises the risk of hypertension, AF and stroke.

4-7-8 breathing: in through the nose for 4 seconds, hold 7, out slowly through the mouth for 8; repeat 4 times. Breathing at about 6 breaths per minute (for example 5 s in, 5 s out) for 5–10 minutes raises HRV in the moment and helps with stress and falling asleep.
entries.source: Zaccaro et al., Front Hum Neurosci 2018

entries.text: One short night can be partly made up with an earlier bedtime or a short nap, but chronic short sleep is not repaid by weekend lie-ins. After a short night, avoid hard training if possible, keep caffeine before noon, and go to bed earlier rather than sleeping very late the next morning.

WHO 2020: adults should do 150–300 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity (or a mix), plus muscle-strengthening for all major muscle groups on 2 or more days. Any amount beats none and benefits keep rising to about 300 minutes. Adults 65+ should add balance training on 3 or more days.

Mortality risk falls steeply from about 2,500 steps a day up to 6,000–8,000 for adults over 60 and 8,000–10,000 for younger adults, then levels off. 10,000 is a fine goal but not a threshold; each extra 1,000 steps a day is linked to roughly 15% lower all-cause mortality.
entries.source: Paluch et al., Lancet Public Health 2022; Banach et al., EJPC 2023

entries.text: Moderate intensity means you can talk but not sing (about 3–6 METs, such as brisk walking at 5–6 km/h); vigorous means only a few words at a time (above 6 METs, such as running, fast cycling or HIIT). One minute of vigorous activity counts about the same as two of moderate toward the weekly target.

Zone 2 is steady effort at about 60–70% of heart-rate reserve where you can still talk in full sentences. It builds aerobic capacity with little fatigue; 2–4 sessions of 30–60 minutes a week lower resting heart rate and raise VO2max over 8–12 weeks.

High-intensity interval training (for example 4 × 4 minutes at 85–95% of max heart rate with 3 minutes easy, or 20 s hard / 10 s rest Tabata) raises VO2max quickly. Keep it to 1–3 sessions a week with at least 48 hours between them, put it on good-recovery days, and skip it when HRV is well below baseline or you are ill.
entries.source: Helgerud et al. 2007; Milanović et al., Sports Med 2015

entries.text: Muscle-strengthening on 2 or more days a week is linked to 10–20% lower all-cause mortality and protects bones, blood sugar control and joints. A simple plan: 2–3 sets of 8–15 reps of squats, push-ups, lunges, rows and planks, stopping each set 1–3 reps short of failure; progress by adding reps, sets or load.

Sitting more than about 8 hours a day raises cardiometabolic risk; 60–75 minutes of moderate activity a day largely offsets it. Break up sitting every 30–60 minutes with 2–5 minutes of walking or stairs.

Warm up for 5–10 minutes before hard sessions: easy cardio until slightly breathless, then dynamic moves (leg swings, lunges, arm circles) and a few build-up reps of the main exercise. Cool down for 5–10 minutes with easy movement; static stretching fits best after training or in its own mobility session.

Delayed-onset muscle soreness peaks 24–72 hours after unfamiliar or eccentric exercise and fades within 5–7 days. Light movement, sleep and protein help; soreness is not a measure of a good workout. Sharp pain, joint swelling, or dark cola-coloured urine after extreme exercise is not soreness — the last can mean rhabdomyolysis and needs urgent care.

Use morning recovery signals together: HRV near or above baseline, resting heart rate at or below baseline and 7+ hours of sleep support a hard session. Two or more signals off (HRV more than 10–15% down, resting heart rate 5+ bpm up, sleep under 6 hours) suggest an easy session or rest. How you feel counts too.
entries.source: Plews et al. 2013; Kiviniemi et al. 2007

entries.text: Signs of overreaching: performance falling despite training, a resting heart rate that stays up, HRV suppressed for a week or more, poor sleep, irritability, heavy legs and frequent colds. Cut training volume by 30–50% for 1–2 weeks; most people recover within days to weeks. Plan an easier week every 3–4 weeks.

Raise weekly training volume by about 10% or less and change one thing at a time (duration, frequency or intensity). Sudden spikes — more than about 1.5 times the average load of the previous 4 weeks — raise injury risk.

"Neck check": if symptoms are only above the neck (runny nose, mild sore throat), light exercise at reduced intensity is usually fine. With symptoms below the neck (fever, chest congestion, body aches, diarrhoea) rest until 24–48 hours after they resolve. After a fever or COVID-type illness, return gradually over 1–2 weeks and stop for chest pain or palpitations.

In heat, drink before you are thirsty, slow down and train in cooler hours. Heat exhaustion (heavy sweating, dizziness, nausea, headache) means stop, cool off and drink. Heat stroke — body temperature above 40 °C with confusion or collapse — is an emergency.

For sessions over an hour, drink about 400–800 mL per hour depending on sweat rate, with some sodium in heat or long efforts. Weighing before and after shows sweat loss: replace each kilogram lost with about 1.25–1.5 L over the next hours.

VO2max is the most oxygen the body can use, in mL/kg/min, and one of the strongest predictors of longevity: moving up from the lowest fitness group brings the largest drop in mortality risk. Apple Watch estimates it from outdoor walks, runs and hikes with heart rate, so it needs regular outdoor activity to stay current.
entries.source: Mandsager et al., JAMA Netw Open 2018; Ross et al., AHA statement 2016

entries.text: VO2max rises fastest with easy volume (zone 2, 2–4 sessions a week) plus one or two interval sessions such as 4 × 4 minutes at 85–95% of max heart rate; untrained people commonly gain 10–20% in 8–12 weeks. Losing excess body fat also raises the per-kilogram value.

Balance and leg strength prevent falls, the leading cause of injury in older adults. Practise standing on one leg (aim for 10+ seconds; failing at age 50–75 is linked to higher mortality), heel-to-toe walking and sit-to-stand from a chair.
Static stretches held 30–60 seconds per muscle group, 2–3 days a week, improve range of motion. Mobility work matters most for joints stiffened by sitting: hips, upper back, ankles and shoulders.
A 10–15 minute walk within 30 minutes after a meal lowers the post-meal glucose rise by roughly 20–30% in many people, with the biggest effect after the largest meal of the day.
entries.source: Buffey et al., Sports Med 2022; Reynolds et al., Diabetologia 2016

entries.text: Fasting plasma glucose below 5.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) is normal; 5.6–6.9 mmol/L is prediabetes by ADA (WHO and China use 6.1–6.9 for impaired fasting glucose); 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or more on two occasions indicates diabetes. mg/dL ÷ 18 = mmol/L.
entries.source: ADA Standards of Care 2025; WHO; Chinese Diabetes Society 2024

entries.text: Two hours after a meal (or a 75 g glucose test), below 7.8 mmol/L is normal, 7.8–11.0 is impaired glucose tolerance, and 11.1 mmol/L or more indicates diabetes. People without diabetes wearing a CGM usually stay under about 7.8–8.9 mmol/L after meals and spend most of the day between 3.9 and 7.8.

HbA1c reflects average glucose over about 3 months: below 5.7% (39 mmol/mol) is normal, 5.7–6.4% is prediabetes, and 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more indicates diabetes. Most adults with diabetes aim for below 7%.

Prediabetes can often be reversed: losing 5–7% of body weight plus 150 minutes of brisk activity a week cut progression to type 2 diabetes by 58% in the Diabetes Prevention Program. Recheck glucose or HbA1c every year.

Glucose below 3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) is low; symptoms are shakiness, sweating, hunger, a fast heartbeat and confusion. Use the 15-15 rule: take 15 g of fast sugar (juice, glucose tablets), recheck after 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then eat a snack. Below 3.0 mmol/L or with confusion it is serious.

To flatten glucose spikes: eat vegetables and protein before starches, choose whole grains and legumes over white rice, white bread and sugary drinks, eat fruit whole rather than as juice, and walk after meals. Pairing carbs with fibre, fat or protein slows absorption.
entries.source: Shukla et al., Diabetes Care 2015; ADA

entries.text: LDL cholesterol: below 2.6 mmol/L optimal, 2.6–3.3 near optimal, 3.4–4.0 borderline high, 4.1–4.8 high, 4.9 or more very high (possible familial hypercholesterolaemia). People with diabetes or heart disease have lower targets (below 1.8 or 1.4) set by their doctor. mg/dL ÷ 38.67 = mmol/L.
entries.source: NCEP ATP III; Chinese Lipid Guidelines 2023; ESC 2019

entries.text: HDL below 1.0 mmol/L in men or 1.3 mmol/L in women is low. Fasting triglycerides below 1.7 mmol/L are normal, 1.7–2.2 borderline, 2.3–5.6 high, and above 5.6 very high with a risk of pancreatitis. Triglycerides fall with less sugar and alcohol, weight loss and exercise.
entries.source: NCEP ATP III; Chinese Lipid Guidelines 2023

entries.text: To lower LDL: swap saturated fat (fatty meat, butter, lard, palm oil) for unsaturated fats (olive or canola oil, nuts, fish), eat 5–10 g of soluble fibre a day (oats, beans, barley) and add plant sterols; together these cut LDL by 10–20%. For most people dietary cholesterol from eggs matters less than saturated fat.
entries.source: AHA 2021 dietary guidance; Jenkins et al., JAMA 2003

entries.text: Serum uric acid above 420 µmol/L (7 mg/dL) is hyperuricaemia by China's definition (some labs use 360 µmol/L for women). Gout attacks are sudden, very painful swollen joints, often the big toe. Risk rises with beer and spirits, sugary drinks and fructose, organ meats, shellfish, dehydration and obesity; low-fat dairy, coffee, cherries and weight loss help.

Metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver (MASLD, formerly NAFLD) affects about a third of adults in China and is driven by excess weight, insulin resistance and alcohol. Losing 7–10% of body weight improves liver fat and inflammation; avoid sugary drinks and limit alcohol. An ALT above the lab range on repeat tests should be reviewed.

Kidney function is screened with eGFR (below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² for 3 months indicates chronic kidney disease) and urine albumin. High blood pressure and diabetes are the main causes; control them, avoid long-term high-dose painkillers such as ibuprofen, and stay hydrated.

BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)². WHO: below 18.5 underweight, 18.5–24.9 normal, 25–29.9 overweight, 30+ obese. China uses lower cut-offs because risk rises at lower BMI in Asian people: 18.5–23.9 normal, 24–27.9 overweight, 28+ obese. BMI cannot tell muscle from fat, so very muscular people can read high.

Waist size measures abdominal fat, which drives metabolic risk more than weight does. Central obesity in China is a waist of 90 cm or more for men and 85 cm or more for women (IDF uses 90/80 for Asian populations). Measure midway between the lowest rib and the top of the hip bone after breathing out. A waist under half your height is a good target for anyone.
entries.source: China NHC; IDF 2006; Ashwell et al. 2012

entries.text: Typical body fat (ACE): men — athletes 6–13%, fit 14–17%, average 18–24%, obese 25%+; women — athletes 14–20%, fit 21–24%, average 25–31%, obese 32%+. Essential fat is about 2–5% in men and 10–13% in women. Smart-scale readings swing with hydration, so compare at the same time of day.

A sustainable pace is about 0.5–1% of body weight a week (roughly 0.25–1 kg). Faster loss tends to cost muscle and is hard to keep; combine a moderate deficit of about 300–500 kcal a day with high protein and strength training. Unintended loss of 5% or more in 6–12 months should be checked by a doctor.

Body weight swings 0.5–2 kg from day to day with water, salt, carbohydrate stores and bowel contents. Weigh at the same time (after waking and the bathroom, before eating) and judge the 7-day average or the trend over 2–4 weeks.
From about age 30–40 adults lose roughly 3–8% of muscle per decade unless they train it, faster after 60. Strength training plus enough protein (1.0–1.6 g/kg a day) slows or reverses this at any age.

0.8 g/kg a day prevents deficiency in sedentary adults; 1.2–1.6 g/kg a day is better for active people, when building muscle, during weight loss and for adults over 65. Spread it over 3–4 meals of about 25–40 g (0.3–0.4 g/kg per meal).

Adults should eat 25–30 g of fibre a day (China recommends the same); most eat about half that. Each extra 8 g a day is linked to 5–27% lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer. Sources: vegetables, legumes, whole grains, fruit and nuts.
entries.source: Reynolds et al., Lancet 2019; Chinese Dietary Guidelines 2022

entries.text: Keep salt below 5 g a day (2 g sodium), which is also China's guideline; average intake in China is about 9–10 g. Most comes from soy sauce, pickles, processed meat, instant noodles and restaurant food. Cutting salt lowers blood pressure within weeks.

Keep free sugars below 10% of energy, ideally below 5% — about 25 g (6 teaspoons) a day. A 500 mL sugary drink holds about 50 g; a large milk tea can hold 30–60 g. Sugary drinks are linked to weight gain, type 2 diabetes, fatty liver, gout and tooth decay.

Total water needs are about 2.0 L a day for women and 2.5 L for men from drinks and food (EFSA); China's guideline suggests 1.5–1.7 L of drinks a day. More is needed in heat, at altitude and with exercise. Pale yellow urine is a good practical guide.

No level of alcohol is risk-free for health (WHO 2023). If drinking, keep to no more than about 1 standard drink a day for women and 2 for men (China: 15 g of alcohol a day at most), with alcohol-free days. Alcohol raises blood pressure, triglycerides, AF risk, liver fat and cancer risk, and disrupts sleep.

Eat fish, ideally oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines), about twice a week for EPA and DHA. Supplements lower very high triglycerides but have shown little benefit against heart attacks in healthy people; check with a doctor if you take blood thinners.

Vitamin D comes from sunlight on the skin and a few foods. Blood 25(OH)D below 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) is often called insufficient and below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL) deficient. Typical adult intake recommendations are 600–800 IU (15–20 µg) a day; do not exceed 4,000 IU a day without medical advice.

Adults need about 800 mg calcium a day (China) or 1,000–1,200 mg (US, more for women over 50 and adults over 70). Dairy, calcium-set tofu, leafy greens and small fish with bones are good sources; get most from food. Strength and impact exercise, vitamin D and not smoking protect bone density.

A practical plate: half vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grains or potatoes, a quarter protein (fish, poultry, beans, tofu, eggs, lean meat), with water to drink. China's Dietary Guidelines suggest 300–500 g vegetables, 200–350 g fruit, 300–500 g dairy and 25–35 g soy and nuts a day.
entries.source: Chinese Dietary Guidelines 2022; Harvard Healthy Eating Plate

entries.text: Higher intake of ultra-processed foods (packaged snacks, sweet drinks, processed meats, instant meals) is linked to weight gain, type 2 diabetes, heart disease and depression; in a controlled trial people ate about 500 kcal a day more on an ultra-processed diet. Cook simple meals from whole ingredients most days.
entries.source: Hall et al., Cell Metab 2019; Lane et al., BMJ 2024

entries.text: Eating most calories earlier and leaving 2–3 hours between dinner and bed helps sleep, reflux and glucose control. Time-restricted eating (for example an 8–10 hour window) helps mainly by reducing total intake.
entries.source: Lowe et al., JAMA IM 2020; Liu et al., NEJM 2022

entries.text: Before training, a light snack with carbohydrate 1–3 hours earlier helps performance. Afterwards about 20–40 g of protein plus carbohydrate within a few hours supports recovery; the daily protein total matters more than exact timing.
entries.source: ISSN Position Stand on nutrient timing 2017

entries.text: Stress raises resting heart rate and lowers HRV through the sympathetic nervous system; chronic stress worsens sleep, blood pressure and blood sugar. Regular exercise, sleep, social contact, time outdoors and slow-breathing or meditation practice all lower physiological stress markers.

Eight-week mindfulness programs reduce anxiety, depression and perceived stress with moderate effect sizes in meta-analyses; even 10 minutes a day helps. Apple Watch Mindfulness sessions count as mindful minutes in Health.
entries.source: Goyal et al., JAMA Intern Med 2014

entries.text: Burnout shows as exhaustion, cynicism or detachment, and reduced effectiveness, often with poor sleep and frequent illness. Protect sleep and recovery time, set limits on working hours, take real breaks, and talk to a professional if it lasts for weeks.

Two screening questions (PHQ-2): over the last 2 weeks, have you often had little interest or pleasure in doing things, or felt down, depressed or hopeless? If either happens on more than half the days, talk to a doctor or counsellor. Exercise is an effective treatment for mild to moderate depression.
entries.source: Kroenke et al. 2003; Noetel et al., BMJ 2024

entries.text: Anxiety often shows up in the body: a fast heartbeat, tight chest, rapid breathing, stomach upset. Long, slow out-breaths calm the nervous system within minutes; anxiety that limits daily life responds well to CBT.

Strong social connection is linked to about 50% better odds of survival in meta-analyses, comparable to quitting smoking. Regular contact with friends and family, volunteering and group exercise all count.

Typical follow-up after eye surgery: LASIK/SMILE at 1 day, 1 week, 1 month, 3 months and 6–12 months, then yearly; cataract surgery at 1 day, 1 week and 4–6 weeks; retinal or glaucoma surgery on the surgeon's schedule. Keep every appointment even when vision feels fine, because pressure changes and inflammation can be silent.

entries.topic: Caring for your eyes after surgery
entries.text: After refractive or cataract surgery: use drops exactly as prescribed, do not rub the eye, keep water, soap and make-up out for 1–2 weeks, wear sunglasses outdoors, and avoid swimming and contact sports for about 2–4 weeks or as advised. Dry eye is common for 3–6 months after LASIK; preservative-free artificial tears help.

Use the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes look at something 6 m (20 feet) away for 20 seconds. Blink fully, keep the screen about an arm's length away and slightly below eye level, and cut glare. Children benefit from 2 hours outdoors a day to slow myopia.

Dry eye causes burning, grittiness, redness and fluctuating vision, worse with screens, air-conditioning and after LASIK. Use preservative-free artificial tears, take screen breaks, use a humidifier, and see an ophthalmologist if it persists.

Adults without symptoms should have a full eye exam every 1–2 years, yearly after 60 or with diabetes, high myopia or a family history of glaucoma. High myopia (beyond −6 D) raises the risk of retinal detachment and glaucoma even after laser correction, because the eye's shape does not change.

Take medicines at the same time each day tied to a routine such as breakfast, and use Health app reminders. Do not stop blood-pressure, cholesterol, antidepressant or other long-term medicines on your own when the numbers look good — that usually means the medicine is working.

For a missed dose, follow the leaflet or ask a pharmacist. A common rule is to take it when you remember unless the next dose is almost due, in which case skip it. Never take a double dose to make up for a missed one.

Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs can raise blood pressure, irritate the stomach and strain the kidneys, especially with dehydration or long-term use. Paracetamol (acetaminophen) is gentler on the stomach but has a strict daily maximum, usually 4 g for healthy adults and lower with regular alcohol use or liver disease.

Grapefruit interacts with some statins, blood-pressure and other medicines; alcohol interacts with sedatives, painkillers and metformin; St John's wort interacts with many drugs. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about every supplement you take.

Common adult screening (varies by country): blood pressure at least yearly; lipids every 4–6 years from age 20–40 and more often with risk; fasting glucose or HbA1c every 3 years from 35–45, earlier with overweight; colorectal screening from 45–50; cervical screening from 21–25; breast imaging from 40–50; low-dose CT for heavy smokers aged 50–80. China recommends a yearly physical exam for adults.
entries.source: USPSTF; Chinese expert consensus on health check-ups

entries.text: Adults benefit from a yearly flu vaccine, a tetanus booster every 10 years, and, depending on age, pneumococcal and shingles vaccines from 50–65. COVID boosters follow current national advice.

Most low back pain is non-specific and improves within 2–6 weeks. Staying active and walking beat bed rest; heat and short-term anti-inflammatories can help. Get urgent care for numbness around the groin, loss of bladder or bowel control, leg weakness, fever, or pain after a major fall.
entries.source: NICE NG59; Lancet Low Back Pain Series 2018

entries.text: Desk neck and shoulder pain improves with the screen at eye level, elbows supported, regular changes of position, and strengthening the upper back (rows, band pull-aparts) 2–3 times a week.

Smoking doubles to quadruples the risk of heart disease and stroke and causes most lung cancer. Quitting at any age helps: heart-attack risk halves within about a year and stroke risk approaches a non-smoker's within 5–15 years. Nicotine replacement plus counselling more than doubles quit rates; e-cigarettes are not risk-free.

Training can continue through the whole cycle. Some feel stronger in the follicular phase and find heat and hard efforts tougher in the luteal phase. Very heavy bleeding (soaking a pad or tampon every 1–2 hours), periods absent for 3+ months without pregnancy, or severe pain should be checked; under-eating in athletes can stop periods.
entries.source: McNulty et al., Sports Med 2020; IOC RED-S 2023

entries.text: Healthy pregnant people should aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity a week; avoid contact sports, lying flat on the back for long after the first trimester, and overheating. Stop and seek care for bleeding, fluid leakage, chest pain, dizziness or regular painful contractions.

Best-supported ways to support immunity: enough sleep (under 6 hours raised the chance of catching a cold about four-fold after virus exposure), regular moderate exercise, vaccines, a balanced diet and not smoking. Megadoses of vitamin C or zinc have small effects at best.

Use broad-spectrum SPF 30+ on exposed skin when the UV index is 3 or more, reapply every 2 hours outdoors, and wear UV400 sunglasses — especially after eye surgery. Check moles for asymmetry, irregular borders, colour change, size over 6 mm or any change over time.
Brush twice a day for 2 minutes with fluoride toothpaste, clean between the teeth daily, and see a dentist every 6–12 months. Gum disease is linked to diabetes and heart disease.

Keep headphone volume below about 60% and limit exposure above 85 dB (heavy traffic) to under 8 hours; the Noise and headphone audio levels in Health track this. Ringing ears after loud events is a warning sign of damage.

Shift sleep by about an hour a day toward destination time before travel, seek morning light after flying east and evening light after flying west, keep caffeine early and skip alcohol on the flight. Low-dose melatonin (0.5–3 mg) at the destination bedtime can help after eastward flights.

Vita's recovery score (0–100) combines last night's HRV against its 30-day baseline, resting heart rate against its baseline, and sleep. 67–100 is green (hard training is fine), 34–66 yellow (train moderately), 0–33 red (rest, walk, mobility and an early night). It is an estimate, not a medical measurement.

Vita's heart age is an estimate from resting heart rate and VO2max compared with typical values for your age and sex. Lowering resting heart rate and raising VO2max with regular aerobic training brings it down; it is not a diagnosis.
Vita's stress index (0–100) is the inverse of recovery: HRV against its baseline, adjusted by resting heart rate and sleep. It is not a laboratory measure of stress.

Chest pain or pressure lasting more than a few minutes — especially spreading to the arm, jaw, neck or back, or with sweating, breathlessness, nausea or faintness — can be a heart attack. Call emergency services now (China 120, EU 112, US 911); do not drive yourself.

Stroke signs (BE FAST): sudden loss of Balance, loss of vision in one or both Eyes, Face drooping, Arm or leg weakness, Speech slurred — Time to call emergency services immediately (China: 120, "中风120"). Note when symptoms began; treatment within 4.5 hours can prevent disability. Do not wait to see if it passes.
Severe shortness of breath at rest, being unable to speak in full sentences, blue lips, or blood oxygen of 90% or less needs emergency care now.

Fainting during exercise, with chest pain or palpitations, after a head injury, or without a clear cause needs urgent medical assessment — exercise-related fainting can signal a dangerous heart rhythm. A simple faint after standing a long time or seeing blood usually recovers within a minute lying down with the legs raised.

If you are thinking about suicide or harming yourself, contact emergency services or a crisis line now and tell someone you trust. China: Beijing psychological crisis hotline 010-82951332 or 400-161-9995, or 120; US: 988; elsewhere, your local emergency number. You do not have to go through this alone.
entries.source: WHO; Beijing Suicide Research and Prevention Center

entries.text: Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing or swallowing, hives with faintness, or collapse after a food, sting or medicine is anaphylaxis: use an adrenaline auto-injector if available and call emergency services immediately.

Blood pressure above 180/120 mmHg: rest for 5 minutes and measure again. If it stays that high with chest pain, breathlessness, back pain, weakness or numbness, vision change, confusion or a severe headache, call emergency services. Without symptoms, contact a doctor the same day.

Glucose below 3.0 mmol/L, or low blood sugar with confusion, a seizure or inability to swallow, is an emergency. If the person can swallow give fast sugar; if not, give nothing by mouth — use glucagon if available and call emergency services.
Fever with a stiff neck, severe headache, sensitivity to light, confusion, or a rash that does not fade when pressed with a glass can be meningitis or sepsis: seek emergency care immediately.

Sudden loss of vision, a curtain or shadow over part of the view, a shower of new floaters or flashes, or severe eye pain with redness, headache and nausea needs same-day emergency eye care — these can be retinal detachment, a stroke in the eye or acute glaucoma. After eye surgery, also report increasing pain, redness or worsening vision at once.

Vomiting blood or material like coffee grounds, black tarry stools, or a lot of blood from the bowel needs emergency care, especially with dizziness or fainting. Iron supplements and bismuth can darken stools, but they are not sticky and tarry.

Heat stroke — body temperature above 40 °C with confusion, collapse or hot skin after heat or exercise — is life-threatening: call emergency services and cool the person at once with cold water, ice packs at the neck, armpits and groin, and fanning.
